sources.title: Steven Hahn, From Radical to Right-Wing: The Legacy of Eugene Genovese
sources.citation: Steven Hahn, “From Radical to Right-Wing: The Legacy of Eugene Genovese,” The New Republic,2October2012; date independently reopened on original by reviewer.

verification.note: Fresh original TNR complete article body retrieved200 and read; ignored original HTML and paragraph witness. Retrospective own undergraduate teaching testimony atP2–3 and continuing pedagogyP11. Includes serious political/personal objections and reports unnamed critics, which are not all converted into Hahn’s own conceptual criticism. No independent reading of cited Genovese books.

sources.title: Steven Hahn, edited Democratic Constitution conversation
sources.citation: “Steven Hahn on Centuries of American Radicalism and Freedom Struggles,” The Democratic Constitution Blog,4September2026, edited interview transcript.

verification.note: Fresh public complete main edited conversation read, with questions and Hahn’s attributed replies distinguished from reader comments. OwnP4 expressly names Thompson and Gutman social history as influences; does not date Hahn’s first reading to the1960s. Printed “Christopher Lash” is transcription spelling; canonical Christopher Lasch not silently treated as a different individual.2026 retrospective cannot be an original formative publication. Speculative political/historical claims remain interview positions, not independent factual endorsements.

sources.title: Gene Santoro interview with Steven Hahn, Political Worlds
sources.citation: Gene Santoro, “Interview: Steven Hahn / The Political Worlds of Slavery and Freedom,” originally American History,June2009; HistoryNet web manifestation21March2018,updated10June2024.

verification.note: Fresh complete public Q&A body read and archived locally. First answerP3 explicitly deploys Du Bois’s general-strike account for Hahn’s own slave-rebellion interpretation. The source’s closing original-publication statement distinguishes2009 interview from2018/2024 web dates. Full Political Worlds and Black Reconstruction remain unread. Interview propositions about maroons and slavery everywhere remain attributed interpretations, not universal factual endorsements.

sources.title: Steven Hahn, review of Eric Foner’s The Fiery Trial
sources.citation: Steven Hahn, review of Eric Foner, The Fiery Trial: Abraham Lincoln and American Slavery, The New Republic,online13January2011; print3February2011.

verification.note: Fresh full original public review body read. OwnP46 explicitly disagrees with Foner’s optimistic counterfactual tendency about Lincoln’s Reconstruction;P5–7/18/35 praise the book and its policy analysis. P37–39 stresses enslaved political initiative while acknowledging Foner includes it. Foner’s book itself unread; no claim the disagreement demonstrates Foner ignored slaves or that the counterfactual can be proved.

sources.title: Steven Hahn, Divine Rights
sources.citation: Steven Hahn, “Divine Rights,” The New Republic,print6February2006, review of Elizabeth Fox-Genovese and Eugene D.Genovese, The Mind of the Master Class(2005), and Erskine Clarke, Dwelling Place(2005).

verification.note: Fresh complete original public review read. Book2005 is distinct from review print2006; local discovery filename2005 is not publication authority. Both Genoveses retain coauthor credit. P14–26 criticises representativeness, undemonstrated hegemony, theology, gender and absent enslaved participants;P15/18 retain praise. P28–46 uses Clarke as positive relational alternative while acknowledging atypicality. All reviewed original monographs unread here.
